title: Privacy timeline source index

anchors.label: Latin privatus/privare lineage noted in private-related scholarship
anchors.description: Privacy is likely a much later noun stabilized in modern English; roots are linked through private/seclusion traditions.
anchors.notes: Indirect and often secondary reconstruction in this pass.

anchors.label: Private / privacy-adjacent terms appear in moral and social meaning fields
anchors.description: Historical dictionary traditions describe private as opposed to public or common exposure in pre-modern records.
anchors.source: Historical dictionary references and usage guides
anchors.notes: Needs direct primary verification in a later pass.

anchors.label: Early public/private distinction appears in legal and social writing
anchors.description: Scholarly framing of privacy as seclusion vs exposure becomes increasingly explicit.
anchors.notes: Keep as directional; not fixed to a single definitive source line yet.

anchors.label: Warren and Brandeis publish 'The Right to Privacy'
anchors.description: The article frames privacy as a legal right against unjustified intrusion.
anchors.source: Warren & Brandeis, The Right to Privacy

anchors.label: Information privacy terminology gains traction in mid-century governance discourse
anchors.description: The term family begins to treat privacy as informational control rather than only seclusion.
anchors.source: Privacy policy histories and archival legal summaries

anchors.label: Domestic/privacy-of-home framing appears in family and personal life contexts
anchors.description: Privacy remains linked to family, home, and bodily/person-based protection.
anchors.source: Secondary legal and social science summaries

anchors.label: U.S. Privacy Act
anchors.description: Federal regulations begin restricting agency handling of records and personal data governance.

anchors.label: OECD data protection guidance for automated processing
anchors.description: OECD starts shaping international data-protection and personal-information language.
anchors.notes: Policy-level anchor rather than a single source quote in this pass.

anchors.label: Privacy language begins to be associated with automated and database systems
anchors.description: Data banking, records systems, and computer processing expand the privacy vocabulary.
anchors.source: Technical/legal overviews on U.S./U.K. data governance
anchors.notes: Category proxy; supports transition into information-technology contexts.

anchors.label: Internet-era usage introduces privacy as online activity concern
anchors.description: Commercial web adoption drives user-facing privacy language around cookies, tracking, and account safety.
anchors.source: Web policy histories and privacy concept pages

anchors.label: Privacy policy and settings interfaces become user-facing in platforms
anchors.description: Online services increasingly expose privacy settings and policy controls to end-users.
anchors.source: Platform terms history and consumer privacy literature
anchors.notes: Needs product-level primary-page audit in later pass.

anchors.label: Security and surveillance language tightens with post-9/11 governance
anchors.description: Institutional security concerns increase public focus on surveillance/privacy trade-offs.

anchors.label: Breach-disclosure reporting begins to normalize privacy-security discourse
anchors.description: Privacy/security risk language strengthens as breach notices and protections expand.
anchors.source: Policy briefings and breach reporting frameworks
anchors.notes: Broad marker, year precision is low.

anchors.label: Post-Snowden public discourse broadens around surveillance and personal autonomy
anchors.description: Large-scale surveillance disclosures become a major reference point for privacy debates.
anchors.notes: Directional event marker, not a single legal anchor.

anchors.label: GDPR enforcement era expands consumer-facing privacy consciousness
anchors.description: Regulatory framework accelerates global references to consent, rights, and platform duties.
anchors.notes: High-confidence anchor with stable legal source.

anchors.label: Targeted advertising and social profiling scandals intensify privacy attention
anchors.description: Data use and microtargeting controversies reshape public language around privacy.
anchors.notes: Media-driven marker; useful for event annotation.

anchors.label: U.S. state privacy regulation enters mainstream product and press attention
anchors.description: CCPA introduces state-level consumer privacy rights framing and private-sector obligations.
anchors.notes: Use as policy-growth anchor, not corpus evidence.

anchors.label: Biometric and generative-model privacy concerns move into policy and rights discussions
anchors.description: AI and biometric analytics create privacy tensions around inference, identity, and automated profiling.
anchors.notes: Early and high-uncertainty, especially in exact year placement.

anchors.label: Search-intent measures remain a recommended future anchor source
anchors.description: Search trend proxies are valuable for post-2020 attention but require a stable acquisition method.
anchors.notes: Placeholder anchor; not date-grounded in this pass.
